questions.stem: Let $\alpha, \beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2 - p x + q = 0$ and $\alpha^4, \beta^4$ be the roots of $x^2 - r x + s = 0$. If $x^2 - 4q x + 2q^2 - r = 0$ has always real roots, then the roots of $x^2 - 4p^2x + 2p^4 - r = 0$ are :
questions.solution:
Let $D_1$ be discriminant of $x^2 - 4qx + 2q^2 - r = 0 \implies 16q^2 - 4(2q^2 - r) = 8q^2 + 4r \ge 0$.
Since $\alpha, \beta$ are roots of $x^2-px+q=0$, we have $q = \alpha\beta$ and $p = \alpha+\beta$.
We have $r = \alpha^4 + \beta^4$.
Let $D_2$ be the discriminant of $x^2 - 4p^2x + 2p^4 - r = 0$.
$D_2 = 16p^4 - 4(2p^4 - r) = 8p^4 + 4r = 8(\alpha+\beta)^4 + 4(\alpha^4+\beta^4) > 0$ as $r > 0$ for non-zero real/complex roots.
Also, product of roots is $2p^4 - r = 2(\alpha+\beta)^4 - (\alpha^4+\beta^4)$.
Since $(\alpha+\beta)^4 \ge 0$, and $2p^4 - r$ can be negative, we check root signs. For real $\alpha, \beta$, $D_2 > 0$ showing roots are real. Product of roots is $2(\alpha+\beta)^4 - (\alpha^4+\beta^4) < 0$ is possible, but carefully analyzing $2p^4 - r$ shows it is positive when $2(\alpha+\beta)^4 > \alpha^4+\beta^4$, which is true by power mean inequality. Thus, product $>0$ and sum $= 4p^2 > 0$, so roots are both positive.
